text: Chapter 9

The private sitting room that Missus Fisher had claimed for herself was charming and full of character. She looked around it with satisfaction after breakfast, glad it was hers. It had a tiled floor, pale honey-colored walls, amber inlaid furniture, and old books, many with ivory or yellow covers. A large window looked out over the sea toward Genoa, and a glass door led onto the castle terrace. She could walk past the quaint watchtower—which had been turned into a small study with chairs and a desk—to a marble seat at the end of the wall. From there, she could see the western bay and the headland leading to the Gulf of Spezia. To the south, between the two stretches of water, was a higher hill at the end of the peninsula, topped by the turrets of a small, empty castle that caught the last rays of the sunset when everything else was in shadow. Yes, she was very comfortable here. The terrace was lined with stone troughs filled with flowers.

She thought this terrace would be the perfect place to walk slowly when her leg wasn't bothering her, or to sit on the cushioned marble bench, if only there hadn't been a second glass door opening onto it. This second door ruined her privacy and her feeling that the terrace was hers alone. It belonged to the round living room, which both she and Lady Caroline had rejected for being too dark. The women from Hampstead would probably use that room, and she was worried they wouldn't just stay inside but would wander onto her terrace. That would ruin the space for her. Even if they didn't walk out, they might still stare at her through the glass. No one could relax knowing they were being watched. What she wanted and deserved was privacy. She didn't want to bother anyone else, so they shouldn't bother her. She could always invite them out later if she grew to like them, but she doubted any of the three would interest her enough to make it worth the effort.

Almost nothing was really worth the effort anymore, Missus Fisher thought, except the past. It was amazing how much better the past was compared to the present. Her friends in London, respectable people of her own age, shared her memories. They could discuss the old days together, compare them to the superficial modern world, and talk about great historical figures instead of the boring, useless young people who seemed to fill the world today. She hadn't left her wise, interesting friends in London just to chat with three young, inexperienced women in Italy; she had only come to escape the cold London April. She had told the two women who came to her house that she just wanted to sit in the sun and reminisce. They knew this, as she had made it very clear. Therefore, she had every right to expect them to stay inside the round living room and not interrupt her on the terrace.

But would they stay inside? This worry ruined her morning. It was only close to lunchtime that she found a solution. She rang for Francesca and, in slow, formal Italian, ordered her to close the wooden shutters on the glass door of the round living room. She went into the room with her, which was now darker than ever. She pointed out to the talking maid that the darkness would keep the room cool, and that there were plenty of narrow windows in the walls for light anyway (though she didn't care if they actually did or not). She then had Francesca help her slide a display cabinet in front of the door from the inside. This would keep people from going out. Next, she called Domenico and had him move one of the large stone flower boxes in front of the door from the outside. This would keep people from coming in.
No one will be able to use this door,
Domenico said, hesitating.
No one will want to,
Missus Fisher replied firmly. She then went back to her sitting room and sat where she could look out at the terrace, feeling pleased that her privacy was now completely secure.

Staying here, she thought calmly, was much cheaper than a hotel and far more pleasant, as long as she could keep the others away. She was paying three pounds a week for her rooms—which came to about eight shillings a day for the bedroom, sitting room, terrace, and watchtower. Where else in Europe could she get all this, plus as many baths as she wanted, for that price? She didn't know yet what the food would cost, but she would insist on keeping the grocery bills low, while still demanding high-quality meals. The two were possible if the person in charge of meals took care. The servants' wages were very low because of the favorable exchange rate, so the food was her only financial worry. If she noticed any waste, she would suggest that they each pay a set weekly amount to Lady Caroline to cover the bills, with any leftover money returned to them, and any extra costs paid by the person who ordered the food.

Missus Fisher was wealthy and liked her comforts, but she hated spending money. She was rich enough to live in a fancy London neighborhood and drive a Rolls-Royce, but she had no interest in that. Managing a large house and a luxury car required more energy than she had. Such possessions brought endless worries, especially bills. In her quiet, gloomy house in Kensington, she could enjoy inexpensive comfort without being bothered by greedy servants or charity collectors, and there was a taxi stand at the end of the street. Her yearly expenses were small. She had inherited the house, and it was furnished with family heirlooms. She walked on her father's old Persian carpet in the dining room and kept time by the black marble clock on the mantelpiece that she had known since childhood. Her walls were covered with signed photos from her famous, deceased friends, and her windows were draped in the same dark red curtains she had always had, alongside the very aquariums she had used for science lessons as a child, where the goldfish of her youth still swam slowly.

Were they the same goldfish? She wasn't sure. Maybe they lived a very long time, or perhaps they had quietly died and been replaced over the years. She sometimes wondered during her solitary dinners if they were the same fish that were there when the writer Carlyle had gotten into a heated argument with her father. He had stormed over to the tank, tapped the glass hard, and yelled at the fleeing fish:
Oh, you deaf devils! You lucky deaf devils! You can't hear any of the nonsense your master is talking, can you?
or something like that.
Carlyle had been such a great soul. He was blunt and direct, which could be shocking in a polite living room, but he was magnificent. No one today could compare to him. Her father had always said,
Thomas is immortal.

Yet the current generation doubted him, or worse, didn't even bother to read him. Missus Fisher didn't read him anymore either, but that was different; she had read him in the past. She remembered a character named Teufelsdröckh—a tailor. It was just like Carlyle to use a name like that. Yes, she must have read his work, even if she forgot the details.

The dinner gong rang. Lost in her memories, Missus Fisher had lost track of time. She hurried to her bedroom to wash her hands and smooth her hair. She didn't want to be late, set a bad example, or find someone else sitting at the head of the table. You couldn't trust the manners of the younger generation, especially Missus Wilkins.

However, she was the first to arrive in the dining room. Francesca, wearing a white apron, stood ready with a huge dish of hot, steaming pasta, but no one was there to eat it. Missus Fisher sat down, looking stern. How disorganized, she thought.
Serve me,

she told Francesca, who wanted to wait for the others. Francesca served her. Of all the ladies, she liked Missus Fisher the least; in fact, she didn't like her at all. She was the only one who hadn't smiled yet. It was true she was old and not pretty, so she had no reason to smile, but nice ladies smiled anyway. They smiled to make others feel welcome. Francesca decided this lady must not be very kind, so she handed her the pasta with a sullen look.

It was well cooked, but Missus Fisher had never liked pasta, especially this long, slippery kind. She found it hard to eat without looking undignified, as the strands wriggled off her fork and hung from her mouth. It always reminded her of her late husband, Mister Fisher. During their marriage, he had behaved very much like pasta—slipping, wriggling, and making her feel foolish. Even when she thought she had him under control, there were always parts of his life that didn't fit. Francesca watched Missus Fisher's struggle from the sideboard, her expression darkening when she saw Missus Fisher take a knife and chop the pasta into small pieces.

Missus Fisher really didn't know how else to eat it. She knew it was bad manners to use a knife on pasta, but she had lost her patience. She never allowed pasta in her London house. She didn't even like it and decided to tell Lady Caroline not to order it again. She thought it must take years of living in Italy to learn how to eat it properly. The poet Robert Browning had managed it beautifully. She remembered watching him eat it at her father's house. It was amazing to watch—no chasing it around the plate or loose ends hanging out. Just one twist, one lift, one bite, and the poet was fed.
Should I go find the young lady?
Francesca asked, unable to watch the pasta being chopped any longer. Missus Fisher snapped out of her memories.
She knows lunch is at twelve-thirty,
she said.
They all do.
She might be asleep,
Francesca said.
The other ladies are far away, but she is nearby.
Ring the gong again then,

Missus Fisher said. What terrible manners, she thought. This wasn't a hotel, and they should show some respect. She was surprised at Missus Arbuthnot, who had seemed punctual. Even Lady Caroline had seemed polite. As for Missus Wilkins, of course, she expected no manners at all.

Francesca fetched the gong and carried it into the garden, banging it loudly as she walked right up to Lady Caroline. Still lying in her chair, Lady Caroline waited until the noise stopped, then turned and spoke in a very sweet voice, though she was actually complaining angrily. Francesca didn't realize she was being scolded, since the voice sounded so musical. Smiling warmly—as she always did when looking at the beautiful girl—she told her the pasta was getting cold.
When I don't come to lunch, it's because I don't want to,
the annoyed Scrap said,
and you must not disturb me in the future.
Are you sick?
Francesca asked sympathetically, still smiling. She had never seen such beautiful hair. It looked like soft, golden silk. Francesca thought she looked like a saint.

Scrap closed her eyes and refused to answer. This was a mistake, as it convinced Francesca that she was sick. The maid hurried to tell Missus Fisher, who said her walking stick kept her from going outside. Instead, she sent the other two women, who had just walked in looking hot, breathless, and apologetic. Meanwhile, Missus Fisher started on the next course—a delicious omelet filled with fresh green peas.
Serve me,
she told Francesca, who wanted to wait for the others.
Oh, why won't they leave me alone?

Scrap asked herself when she heard footsteps on the gravel path, signaling that someone else was coming. She kept her eyes tightly shut. Why should she eat lunch if she didn't want to? This wasn't a family home, and she didn't owe any duties to a host. For all practical purposes, this castle was a hotel, and she should be allowed to skip meals if she wanted to.

But poor Scrap couldn't just close her eyes without making people want to fuss over her. Even the cook had patted her. And now, a gentle hand was placed on her forehead—a gesture she knew and dreaded.
I'm afraid you're not feeling well,
said a voice. It wasn't Missus Fisher, so it had to be one of the Hampstead ladies.
I have a headache,
Scrap murmured, thinking this was the quickest way to be left alone.
I'm so sorry,
Missus Arbuthnot said softly, keeping her hand on her forehead.
And here I thought I would escape motherly fussing by coming to Italy,
Scrap thought to herself.
Don't you think some tea would help?
Missus Arbuthnot asked gently. Tea? Scrap hated the idea of drinking hot tea in the midday heat.
No,
she whispered.
I think the best thing for her is to be left in peace,

another voice said. How sensible, Scrap thought, opening one eye just a crack to see who was speaking. It was the freckled lady. The dark-haired one was the one touching her. Scrap immediately liked the freckled one better.
But I hate to think of you having a headache and doing nothing for it,
Missus Arbuthnot said.
Would a cup of black coffee—?
Scrap said nothing. She waited in silence for Missus Arbuthnot to take her hand away. Eventually she would have to leave.
I really think she just needs quiet,

the freckled one repeated. She must have pulled the other woman's sleeve, because the hand left Scrap's forehead. After a moment of silence—during which they no doubt stared at her, as everyone did—the footsteps faded away down the path.
Lady Caroline has a headache,
Missus Arbuthnot said as she sat back down next to Missus Fisher.
She won't take any tea or coffee. Do you know how to say aspirin in Italian?
The best cure for a headache,
Missus Fisher said firmly,
is castor oil.
But she doesn't have a headache,
Missus Wilkins said.
Carlyle suffered terribly from headaches at one point,
Missus Fisher said, taking the opportunity to share a story.
He took castor oil constantly. He actually called it
the oil of sorrow.
My father said it affected his entire philosophy on life because he took too much. Lady Caroline just needs one dose. It's a mistake to take it regularly.
Do you know the Italian word for it?
Missus Arbuthnot asked.
No, I don't. But she would know. You can ask her.
But she doesn't have a headache,
Missus Wilkins repeated, still struggling to eat her pasta.
She just wants to be left alone.
They both stared at her. Missus Fisher thought Missus Wilkins ate very sloppily.
Then why would she lie about it?
Missus Arbuthnot asked.
Because she's still trying to be polite,
Missus Wilkins explained.
Soon she won't have to try anymore; once she relaxes here, she'll just be naturally honest without trying.
Lotty has a theory about this place—

Missus Arbuthnot explained, smiling at Missus Fisher. Missus Fisher was waiting impatiently for the next course, which was delayed because Missus Wilkins was still trying to eat the cold pasta. But Missus Fisher had no interest in Missus Wilkins's theories.
I don't know why you would assume Lady Caroline is lying,
she interrupted, glaring at Missus Wilkins.
I'm not assuming, I know,
Missus Wilkins said.
And how do you know?
Missus Fisher asked coldly, especially since Missus Wilkins was taking a second helping of pasta.
When I was out there, I saw right through her,
Missus Wilkins said. Missus Fisher decided not to argue with such nonsense. Instead, she rang the table gong sharply, even though Francesca was standing right there, and said,
Serve the next course.
Francesca, likely on purpose, offered her the pasta again.
